title: The Cache Line, the Set, and the Address Split
unit: Memory Interfacing, Hierarchy and Cache Mapping
quickIdea: A cache is a table of lines; each line holds a valid bit, a tag and one block of data. The memory address is cut into tag, index and offset, and the widths of the three cuts follow from the cache size and block size alone.
remember: Offset bits = log2(block size in addressable units). It picks the word inside the line.
Number of lines = cache data size / block size. Number of sets = lines / associativity.
Index bits = log2(number of sets). It picks the set. In a direct-mapped cache sets = lines; in a fully associative cache there is one set, so index = 0 bits.
Tag bits = address width - index bits - offset bits. The tag is what is stored in the directory and compared on a lookup.
A hit needs the valid bit set and the tag equal; the offset then selects the word. The tag does not identify a word, it identifies which memory block is currently sitting in that line.

example.prompt: A 16 KB direct-mapped cache has 32 B blocks and the processor sends 32-bit byte addresses. Give the three field widths.
example.work: Offset = log2 32 = 5. Lines = 16384/32 = 512, so index = 9. Tag = 32 - 9 - 5 = 18.
example.answer: Tag 18, index 9, offset 5 - the split the IISc slides use for exactly this configuration.

gateAngle: Every tag-width question in the last decade is this arithmetic with one twist: the associativity, the word length or the address space changed. Work out the offset first, then the index, then subtract both from the address width.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: A 4-way set-associative cache of 32 KB uses 64 B blocks with 24-bit addresses. Give the three widths and the number of comparators.
variations.answer: Offset 6; lines = 32768/64 = 512; sets = 128, so index 7; tag = 24 - 7 - 6 = 11. Four comparators of 11 bits each.
variations.why: It is the standard arithmetic plus the one hardware consequence: the comparator count equals the associativity.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why does the offset never appear in the tag directory?
variations.answer: Because the offset selects a word inside the line, and the whole line is present or absent as a unit; the directory stores only what identifies the block.
variations.why: It explains why the tag is a block identifier and why the directory is much smaller than the cache.

trap.what: Counting the tag directory as if it held only the tag.
trap.why: Each line also carries a valid bit, often a dirty bit and sometimes replacement bits, so the directory is wider than the tag; questions that ask for directory size expect those bits to be counted.
trap.counterexample: A 256-line cache with 19-bit tags and one valid and one dirty bit needs 256 x 21 = 5376 bits, not 256 x 19 = 4864 - and both numbers appear among the options of the 2011 question.

check.question: An 8 KB 2-way cache uses 32 B blocks and 20-bit addresses. How many sets and what are the three widths?
check.answer: 256 lines, 128 sets, so index 7; offset 5; tag = 20 - 7 - 5 = 8 bits.
check.explanation: Halving the lines by making it 2-way removes exactly one index bit, which the tag gains - the same trade the 2017 question makes with 16 ways.
